newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Humour is students' only weapon in Belgrade protest.
newsitem.headline: Humour is students' only weapon in Belgrade protest.

text.p: Two drummers beat out a frenzied salsa beat on their kettledrums, someone's home-made scarlet top hat bobs above the heads of the crowd, whistles blow, elderly men lift their fedoras in salute.
Another student protest is on the move.

Hundreds of students -- laughing, chattering, smoking, chewing gum, holding hands -- walk swiftly away from the engineering faculty and within minutes another column of architectural students is horn-blowing and whistling.

Contingents of several hundred join up and finally mass in front of the justice ministry in central Belgrade. A heaving sea of several thousand people blocks a vital intersection, halting trams and cars. Uniformed police in peaked caps seem content to watch from a distance and mutter into their radios.
It resembles a huge, free and very noisy outdoor party.

There is little sense of organisation. Self-appointed student stewards, usually male and slightly older than most, jog or sprint back and forth along the route, keeping order of a kind in the ragged ranks.

No one, not even the stewards themselves, seem to know the route in advance. Decisions appear to be taken haphazardly, and at the last possible moment. A sudden flurry of banners and flags in the vanguard is the only sign that the marchers will move left or right.

One young woman sports an enormous red velvet elephant as a hat. It is almost as big as she is with huge ear flaps and even a trunk. She proves to be a favourite target for television crews looking for something different after 75 days of street marches.

The standard uniform seems to be padded anorak, trainers, baseball cap, whistle around the neck and large, brightly coloured lapel badge proclaiming the wearer's university or faculty. Most seem to smoke American cigarettes.
It is bitterly cold. Hanging around in front of the justice ministry while someone tries to deliver a petition to the attorney-general, many students leap up and down in an effort to keep warm.

Bystanders clap, wave, hand over fruit and bread or simply stare. Most people seem happy to see the students and even the bus and tram drivers seemed resigned to the delays the students cause in deliberately blocking busy streets.
How long students can keep up their pro-democracy protests is anyone's guess. But they are clearly having a good time.

"If the protest is going on beyond February 14 it will go on forever because that's the start of the second semester (term) and it would mean the whole year is gone," said Sharkie, a 27-year-old biochemistry student.
What of the socialist government's threat to withhold cash from universities and schools because of the widening dissent?
Uros, 18, says: "It'll just make the students angrier. Our parents support us. It won't make any difference."
And what do the students want changed?
"Everything," says architecture student Ivana. "The whole structure of government needs reform and the university is only part of it."
